Jacqueline Rose

Power Without Authority

As the electoral verdict against Donald Trump and the conviction of Russell Brand occurred side-by-side, their similarities struck a chord.

November 24, 2026

Caitlin L. Chandler

Spain in the Balance

The forces holding back a tide of resurgent right-wing politics in the country are as embattled and divided now as they have ever been.

November 21, 2026

Rachel Donadio

France in Turmoil

Five months before presidential elections in which the extreme right is widely expected to come to power, the country is facing a debt crisis, a political crisis, and a social crisis.

December 17, 2026 issue

Orly Noy

Israel’s Arab Parties Ascendant

The recent elections have posed a question to Israeli society: Is the citizenship of Palestinians genuine?

November 22, 2026

Caroline Moorehead

Home and Away

In her novels Fausta Cialente, an Italian émigré who spent much of her life in Egypt, wrote about rootless women and girls addicted to flight.

December 3, 2026 issue

“How is it that the only president in US history to mount a coup d’état was ushered back to the White House four years later by a plurality of American voters?”

— Mark Danner: The Tightrope Walker

December 3, 2026

Current Issue
Trevor Jackson

The Cost of Monetizing Everything

Behavioral economists prided themselves on bringing rational thinking to public policy, but behind their “nudges” for optimizing consumer behavior was a big corporate push.

December 3, 2026 issue

Michael Gorra

Nightmares of History

The Newer World completes Sebastian Barry’s trilogy of novels about Americans caught up in the violence of the nineteenth century.

December 3, 2026 issue

Darryl Pinckney

Arthur Schomburg’s Legacy

The Schomburg Center in Harlem is marking its centennial by celebrating the man whose library grew into one of the world’s great collections of black history and literature.

December 3, 2026 issue

Jed Perl

Masters of Their Craft

For 150 years Paris was the research hub, testing ground, and production center for modern painting and sculpture.

December 3, 2026 issue

Tim Flannery

‘Quest Without End’

The Scottish journalist Cal Flyn travels the world in search of the feelings that wild and abandoned places evoke.

December 3, 2026 issue

Susan Tallman

Seeing Through the Lightness

Equanimity once defined Brice Marden’s art—optical balance so solid it felt inevitable. In a current survey, maintaining it feels more like a feat, something grabbed in motion.

December 3, 2026 issue

Piper French

The Executioner’s Song

Pamela Colloff’s Catch the Devil is as much the tale of a notorious jailhouse informant who put an innocent man on death row as it is the story of the officials and institutions that encouraged his lies.

December 3, 2026 issue

Clare Carlisle

Reverence for All of It

Benedict de Spinoza’s ideas about the interchangeability of God and nature made him a heretic in seventeenth-century Europe. But would it be correct to call him an atheist today?

December 3, 2026 issue

Helen Epstein and Aminu Abubakar

Interview with a Bandit

Many Nigerians have turned to violence after years of suffering under widespread government corruption.

December 3, 2026 issue

Fintan O’Toole

The Next Generation

The American left has won a historic election by successfully linking the affordability crisis to Republican corruption, and the whole Democratic Party must now learn from their example.

December 3, 2026 issue

Kristen Roupenian

We Tell Ourselves Stories in Order to Change

In the films and fiction of Jane Schoenbrun, the boundary between reality and fantasy is porous, alluring, and must be carefully patrolled.

December 3, 2026 issue

David Shulman

Collateral Damage

In the documentary film NAZA, Israeli soldiers speak candidly about their remorse at participating in the war in Gaza.

December 3, 2026 issue

New Poems

Susana Plotts-Pineda

Our Lady of Beverly, TX

December 3, 2026 issue

Aaron Fagan

Why I Go to the Movies Alone

December 3, 2026 issue

Jenny Grassl

Deer Woman in the Dining Room

November 19, 2026 issue

At the Galleries
Max Norman

The Many Views of Yvonne Jacquette

Her frequent ascents in airplanes and helicopters, and to the tops of skyscrapers, granted the painter an unusual and rich perspective.

November 19, 2026 issue

Jé Wilson

Olana Interrupted

The sublime landscapes that inspired Frederic Edwin Church are refracted through climate change in an outdoor installation by the artist Ellen Harvey.

November 19, 2026 issue

Will Heinrich

Turning Around the Easel

The painter Emily Mae Smith hands over her brush to a character borrowed from pop culture—a gesture with symbolic depth.

November 5, 2026 issue

Read more about At the Galleries
NYR Online
Deborah Eisenberg

The Struggle Has Begun

Will the Democrats seize the chance they’ve been given?

November 18, 2026

Camila Rocha, translated by Sean Purdy

Red, White, Green, Yellow, and Blue

In recent years Brazil’s far right has adopted a surprising rallying cry: voluntary submission to Trump’s US.

November 18, 2026

Katie Kadue

The Ecstasy of Ken Russell

The Devils, newly available in a long-suppressed uncut version, is a film of both extravagant theatricality and surprising sincerity.

November 11, 2026

Christopher Hooks, Francisco Cantú, Aslı Ü. Bâli, and Aziz Rana

The Blue Wave—III

On foreign and domestic affairs, border-town resistance, and the Texas liberal tradition.

November 10, 2026

Rozina Ali, Olivia Paschal, Lily Geismer, and David Treuer

The Blue Wave—II

On crescendoing Islamophobia, the new Southern strategy, the legacy of the Watergate Babies, and remaking the system.

November 9, 2026

David Cole, Sue Halpern, Mark O’Connell, and Quinn Slobodian

The Blue Wave—I

On people power, memes, the view from the North Country, and JD Vance’s double bind.

November 6, 2026

Anne Fadiman

Oysters High and Low

Consider the Oyster is not really about cooking; like all of M.F.K. Fisher’s work, it’s about imagining.

November 3, 2026

David Cole

Are There No Limits to Religious Freedom?

In the Supreme Court’s latest religious-freedom case, a Catholic school argues that the state has a constitutional duty to subsidize its discrimination.

November 2, 2026

Tim Judah

Serbia’s Graduation Day

Last week’s elections delivered Serbia’s students a historic victory over their country’s authoritarian president. What comes next?

November 1, 2026

Read more about NYR Online
New York Review Podcasts
Celia Paul

Celia Paul Reads from Objects of Desire

Season 2, Episode 10 of Private Life

November 25, 2026

Susan Neiman, in conversation with Fintan O’Toole

The Possibility of Progress

Season 1, Episode 7 of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole

November 24, 2026

Celia Paul, in conversation with Jarrett Earnest

Celia Paul on Her Memoir, Life, and Art

Season 2, Episode 9 of Private Life

November 18, 2026

Ben Rhodes and Astra Taylor, in conversation with Fintan O’Toole

When Democrats Became the Populists

Season 1, Episode 6 of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole

November 17, 2026

Brief Encounters
Melissa Anderson, interviewed by Nawal Arjini

In the High Holy Temples of Cinema

“New York City is constantly reborn and reenergized by young people.”

November 14, 2026

Joseph O’Neill, interviewed by Daniel Drake

Now What?

“A mandate is a command, we sometimes forget. It is mandatory for Democrats to respond to the voters’ concerns. If they don’t, their party could soon suffer its own collapse.”

November 7, 2026

Lola Seaton, interviewed by Lauren Kane

Switching On

“The art of receiving art, like the art of making it, seems deeply related to the need to discover what we share.”

October 17, 2026

Matthew Aucoin, interviewed by Daniel Drake

The Composer

“It makes all the difference in the world whether the people performing the music love and believe in it.”

October 10, 2026

More about Brief Encounters

Free from the Archives

M.F.K. Fisher: Yuk!

“Slugs are one of my few innate dislikes, although I am more tolerant of them as I mature. I have eaten them calmly, so as not to lose face, in several Spaces and Times.”

Ghost Stories
Geoffrey O’Brien

A Gust from Another World

The Search for Bridey Murphy caused a sensation in 1950s America, and while its tale of reincarnation was soon discredited, it revealed a deep cultural fascination with the supernatural.

August 20, 2026 issue

Frederick C. Crews

The Consolation of Theosophy

“Like others who pined for lost certainties, W.B. Yeats had fallen under the spell of one of the gaudiest characters of the nineteenth century, Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, co-founder (with Henry Steel Olcott) of the burgeoning Theosophical Society, and a catalyst of unorthodox neo-religious stirrings in America, England, the European continent, India, and elsewhere.”

September 19, 1996 issue

Nell Stevens

Communing with Mrs. Gaskell

Gaining the dead’s permission to write about them was a preoccupation of the Victorian age, and, as my book about Elizabeth Gaskell entered the world, it became mine, too.

October 24, 2018

Jonathan Miller

Going Unconscious

“According to Mesmer, the human nervous system was charged with ‘animal’ magnetism—so-called because it was associated with the soul or anima—and although it was not physically detectable he insisted that it could be mobilized by the will of an initiated practitioner and broadcast to living bodies in the vicinity.”

April 20, 1995 issue

Unsettling, Haunting, Grotesque, Sublime
Matthew Aucoin

A Dance to the Music of Death

Thomas Adès turns fleetingly recognizable musical elements into unstable, volatile substances tending toward evanescence and escape.

May 13, 2021 issue

Anthony Grafton and Ingrid D. Rowland

The Witch Hunters’ Crusade

Why did sixteenth-century investigators of witchcraft place such an inordinate emphasis on demonic sex, and why did they concentrate their inquiries on women?

September 26, 2002 issue

Mike Jay

The Hide That Binds

A medical librarian’s history of books covered in human skin.

November 5, 2020 issue

Nathaniel Rich

Arthur Kern's Creatures

Arthur Kern’s unsettling, grotesque sculptures bring to mind twins fighting for space within the womb, disembodied heads frozen in cryogenic pods, an astronaut doomed to float forever through outer space.

June 1, 2016

Fascist Dorks
Mark O’Connell

Space Oddity

Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff’s Muskism examines how Elon Musk became the world’s first trillionaire, by selling a vision of the future that very few people would want to inhabit.

July 23, 2026 issue

Anne Diebel

The Dungeon Master

Peter Thiel is full of contradictions—a libertarian who founded a company that aids government surveillance, a critic of tech who supports Facebook’s mission for world domination, and a defender of free speech who helped to kill a media outlet.

February 10, 2022 issue

Suzanne Schneider

From the Cesspool to the Mainstream

The “new fusionist” intellectuals are the missing link between nineteenth-century race science, twentieth-century libertarianism, and the contemporary alt-right.

October 23, 2025 issue

Ben Tarnoff

Venture-Backed Trumpism

Why have right-wing ideas found such an eager audience among tech elites during Biden’s presidency?

September 19, 2024 issue

Having a Poem with You
Langdon Hammer

Alert to Reality

The first biography of James Schuyler suggests that his tendency to withdraw was both a harbinger of his disabling mood disorder and the wellspring of his shimmering poetry.

November 20, 2025 issue

Lucy Sante

John Ashbery (1927–2017)

He was lionized, imitated, studied, analyzed, enshrined, revered.

October 12, 2017 issue

Dan Chiasson

Crossing the Invisible Line

The astonishing work of poet Eileen Myles set a bar for openness, frankness, and variability few lives could ever match.

March 24, 2016 issue

Geoffrey O’Brien

The Mayakovsky of MacDougal Street

“One has to go back to fairly remote periods—ancient Rome, eighteenth-century London—to find poetry as meticulous in its gossip and as minute in its urban observation as Frank O’Hara’s.”

December 2, 1993 issue

Advertisement

On Israel and Gaza
Joelle M. Abi-Rached

‘Natives of the Country’

By taking up the cause of Lebanon’s murdered Jewish leaders, Israel threatens to detach them from their history and absorb them into its own.

October 22, 2026

Sophia Goodfriend

Target Practice

Artificial intelligence systems—now an integral part of the Israeli war machine—began as tools developed to surveil every aspect of Palestinian life.

July 23, 2026

Helen Epstein

Gaza’s Deadly Soil

Amid tight Israeli restrictions, new remote research is starting to make visible the scale of toxic fallout across the Gaza Strip.

July 22, 2026

Mary Turfah

Safety Is When There’s No One Dying

Israel’s assault on Palestine and Lebanon has reconfigured how children understand the world.

June 24, 2026

Adania Shibli

Dead Lands

Rather than letting ourselves tire of repeated stories, how might we allow them to inform us about something we couldn’t grasp otherwise?

June 17, 2026

Piper French

To Break the Siege

By sailing to Gaza, activists in the flotilla movement have long tried to pressure their own governments to honor international law. 

May 31, 2026

Neve Gordon

The Gaza Doctrine

Over the course of two years, Israeli forces systematically destroyed the Gaza Strip’s health system. Their attacks in Iran and Lebanon follow a disturbingly similar pattern.

March 22, 2026

Doha Kahlout, translated by Katharine Halls

Elegy for Rafah

For the tens of thousands of Gazans who need to leave the Strip but want the chance to come back home, life revolves around the Rafah crossing.

March 20, 2026
